Backed by marquee names like General Atlantic, Amazon and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), the startup has raised $458 Mn to date. It achieved the unicorn valuation during its $255 Mn Series D fundraise in 2021. 

In April, the startup roped in ICICI Securities, Morgan Stanley, and Kotak Securities as the bankers to helm its upcoming IPO, which will comprise both fresh issue and an OFS. The startup is said to be looking to raise $300 Mn to $400 Mn via its public issue at a likely valuation of $2 Bn to $2.5 Bn.

Acko is looking to file its DRHP via the confidential route in the second half of 2026 and is eyeing a listing in the first half of 2027.

Ahead of its potential D-Street debut, the startup laid off around 60 employees, or nearly 5% of its total workforce, to streamline its operations, citing AI-led automation.

On the financial front, Acko reported a net loss of ₹424.4 Cr in FY25, down 57% from ₹669.9 Cr the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 35% to ₹2,836.8 Cr from ₹2,106 Cr in FY24.

Battery Smart

Founded in 2019 by Pulkit Khurana and Siddharth Sikka, Battery Smart operates a battery-as-a-service platform that enables commercial electric two- and three-wheelers to swap discharged batteries for fully charged ones within minutes.

The startup claims to have built a network of more than 1,500 swapping stations across 75+ cities. It has so far deployed over 3 Lakh lithium-ion batteries and nearly 1 Lakh commercial EV drivers use its network. 

It has raised more than $200 Mn to date from marquee names like Tiger Global, Orios Venture Partners, FAAD Network, Blume Ventures and Trifecta Capital.

Battery Smart’s IPO plans first came to light in August 2026 after reports surfaced that the startup was looking to file its DRHP with SEBI by October 2026. There appears no clarity so far on its public issue size and the valuation it plans to seek.

On the financial front, the startup’s net loss widened nearly 93% to ₹27 Cr in FY25 as against ₹14 Cr in the year ago fiscal. However, revenue from operations zoomed 52% to ₹249 Cr during the fiscal under review compared to ₹164 Cr in FY24.

BRND.ME (Formerly Mensa Brands)

Founded in 2021 by ex-Myntra CEO Ananth Narayanan as Mensa Brands, BRND.ME is a house of brands that initially acquired 20 D2C brands to scale them. It became the fastest Indian startup to enter the unicorn club in 2021, attaining the coveted $1 Bn valuation within six months of its inception. 

It rebranded to its new identity last year and operates consumer brands such as Pebble, MyFitness, Dennis Lingo, among others. The unicorn has raised more than $300 Mn in funding till date from the likes of Accel, Alpha Wave Global, Norwest Venture Partners, Tiger Global, and Prosus.

The company is looking to list on the Indian bourses by 2027. Ahead of the IPO, the unicorn received approvals from National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in February 2026 to redomicile back to India from Singapore. 

On the financial front, BRND.ME saw a 5.8% decline in operating revenue to $168 Mn (about ₹1,394 Cr) in FY25 from $178.6 Mn (about ₹1,482 Cr) in the previous fiscal. Meanwhile, its loss widened 39% to $60.4 Mn (about ₹501 Cr) from $43.5 Mn (about ₹361 Cr) in FY24.  

Captain Fresh

Founded in 2019 by Utham Gowda, Captain Fresh runs a B2B seafood platform that exports fish. It also operates a marketplace that connects fisherfolk with buyers. It also provides end-to-end operations management tools for retail outlets and supermarket chains.

Backed by Tiger Global, Prosus, and British International Investment (BII), the startup has raised over $172 Mn to date.

Captain Fresh took its first official step toward listing in July 2025 by converting to a public entity and dropping the word “private” from its name. Subsequently in August 2025, Inc42 reported that the startup had confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI for a $400 Mn public issue, split between a $200 Mn fresh issue and a $150-200 Mn offer-for-sale.

However, in late December 2025, the startup withdrew its DRHP from SEBI due to delays in regulatory clearances for an acquisition in Europe. Captain Fresh plans to refile papers in early 2026 once approvals are secured.

Captain Fresh flipped to profitability in FY25, posting a consolidated net profit of ₹42.4 Cr as against a loss of ₹229 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Operating revenue skyrocketed 145% to ₹3,421 Cr from ₹1,395 Cr in FY24.

CarDekho

Founded in 2008 by siblings Amit Jain and Anurag Jain, CarDekho Group operates an online car listing platform, insurtech platform InsuranceDekho, lending platform Rupyy, and other brands. 

The startup has so far raised more than $750 Mn in funding to date and competes with the likes of CarTrade, Spinny and Cars24.

CarDekho has been planning to list on the bourses for some time now. At first, it was internally mulling plans for an IPO in 2021, but the idea failed to take off. Afterwards in 2024, the unicorn once again began talks with merchant bankers for a public issue to raise nearly $500 Mn at a valuation of $2 Bn to $2.5 Bn. This plan also failed to materialise. 

The auto marketplace is now back on the IPO bandwagon. It has already lined up Axis Bank, IIFL, Goldman Sachs and Nomura as bankers to helm its listing. It is now looking to file its DRHP by September 2026 to raise up to ₹3,500 Cr via an IPO, which will comprise both fresh issue (10% of the total size) and an OFS. 

The unicorn is said to be eyeing a valuation of ₹13,000-15,000 Cr for the listing, higher than ₹9,000 Cr at which it was pegged during its last fundraise in 2021.

On the financial front, CarDekho Group’s consolidated operating revenue rose 24% YoY to ₹2,795 Cr in FY25, while net loss narrowed marginally to ₹266 Cr from ₹276 Cr in FY24.

Cars24

Founded in 2015 by Vikram Chopra, Gajendra Jangid, Mehul Agrawal, Ruchit Agarwal and Chopra, Cars24 operates an online marketplace that allows users to buy and sell pre-owned cars. 

It has lately also forayed into new segments like auto-focussed content commerce market with Team BHP and vehicle information platform space with CarInfo. Having raised more than $1.3 Bn to date, the startup entered the unicorn club in 2020 after its $200 Mn Series E fundraise. 

The auto tech major’s IPO plans came to light in January 2026 after cofounder and CEO Chopra said that Cars24 would list on the bourses in the next six to twelve months (July 2026 to January 2027). 

However, in September 2026, Cars24 CFO Shivanshu Makkar reportedly said that the used-car marketplace would be able to complete its reverse flip from Singapore to India only by April 2027. It will then file its DRHP for an IPO.

If the plan materialises, Cars24 would become the second auto tech startup to go public, after rival CarTrade. 

On the financial front, Cars24’s operating revenue jumped 25% to ₹6,917.1 Cr in FY24 compared to ₹5,529.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Net losses also rose 7% to ₹498.4 Cr from ₹467.7 Cr in FY23.

Flipkart

Founded in 2007 by Binny Bansal and Sachin Bansal, Flipkart has grown from a small online bookstore into India’s largest ecommerce marketplace. Walmart acquired majority control in the ecommerce juggernaut in 2018 for $16 Bn. Since then, it has also expanded into fintech, travel tech and quick commerce.

Flipkart was last valued at $35 Bn after a $1 Bn fundraise in 2024. Arguably the biggest startup in the country by valuation, the decacorn received in-principle approval from a Singapore court in September 2025 to reverse flip back to India for its IPO. The plan was then cleared by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in December 2025.

Subsequently, the company redomiciled back to India in March 2026 after receiving the nod from the Indian government. A month later, reports surfaced that the ecommerce major was exploring raising a pre-IPO round of $2 Bn to $2.5 Bn from Indian and foreign investors. 

Taking a sharp U-Turn in May 2026, reports surfaced that Flipkart had deferred its IPO till at least 2028 to focus on profitability before its public listing. This came after parent Walmart directed the ecommerce company to focus on achieving EBITDA breakeven in FY27 itself.

The ecommerce major’s B2C arm, Flipkart Internet Private Ltd, reported an operating revenue of ₹20,493 Cr in FY25, up from ₹17,907 Cr in FY24. Meanwhile, losses also narrowed 37% to ₹1,494 Cr from ₹2,359 Cr, showing improved unit economics despite diversification.

Furlenco

Founded in 2012 by Ajith Mohan Karimpana, Furlenco operates a furniture and appliance rental platform across 28 cities like Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Chennai, and Kolkata. With over 300 SKUs, the platform also sells new furniture.

Backed by Sheela Foam, Lightbox Ventures, Crescent Ventures, and White Oak, Furlenco has raised more than $290 Mn to date.

In September 2026, reports surfaced that the furniture and appliance rental startup had kicked off proceedings for a potential ₹1,000-1,200 Cr public issue. Furlenco is said to be close to appointing ICICI Securities as an advisor for its IPO, which will target a valuation of around ₹7,000 Cr. Furlenco is looking to launch the IPO in FY28.

The furniture rental startup turned profitable in FY25, with a net profit of ₹3.1 Cr as against a net loss of ₹130.2 Cr in FY24. Meanwhile, its revenue from operations spiked 64% to ₹228.7 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹139.6 Cr in FY24.

GoBoult

The bootstrapped startup competes with the likes of boAt, Noise and Pebble. GoBoult sells its products via its own website, online marketplaces, quick commerce platforms as well as 3,000 offline stores across India.

Kicking off its IPO plans, GoBoult cofounder Varun Gupta told Inc42 that the smart wearables brand is planning to file its DRHP with SEBI by November 2026. The company is eyeing a listing on the bourses by the summer of 2027. 

On the financial front, GoBoult reported an operating revenue of ₹762.9 Cr in FY25, up 9.4% from ₹697.2 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its profit stood at ₹24.2 Cr during the fiscal, a near 10X jump from ₹2.5 Cr reported in FY24.

After more than a year of suspense, reports once again surfaced in October 2026 that the startup was looking to file its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route by January 2027. Imarticus is now said to be eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr IPO.

On the financial front, Imarticus Learning’s revenue grew over 16% to ₹159 Cr in FY24 from ₹136.8 Cr in FY23, as per Tofler. Net losses, however, shot up nearly 10% to ₹24.6 Cr from ₹22.4 Cr in the year ago fiscal.

InMobi

In July 2026, reports surfaced that the adtech unicorn had roped in four merchant bankers, namely JPMorgan Chase, Jefferies, Kotak Mahindra Capital and Axis Capital, to helm its upcoming $1 Bn (₹9,634 Cr) public issue.

Leverage Edu

The startup claims to have so far catered to more than 1.75 Lakh customers. Leverage Edu has so far raised nearly $73 Mn from names such as Blume Ventures, DSG Consumer Partners, and Kaizenvest.

On the financial front, Leverage Edu’s revenue from operations zoomed 91% to ₹173 Cr in FY25 from ₹90.6 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. In line with the top line, losses also rose nearly 56% to ₹106 Cr from ₹68 Cr in FY25. 

Mohalla Tech (ShareChat)

On the financial front, ShareChat managed to narrow its adjusted EBITDA loss by 72% to ₹219 Cr in FY25 from ₹793 Cr a year ago. However, its operating revenue remained nearly flat at ₹723 Cr as against ₹718 Cr in FY24.

Navi

OfBusiness

This time, it is eyeing a $800 Mn IPO, which could comprise a fresh issue of up to $260 Mn and a $540 Mn OFS. OfBusiness is said to be targeting a valuation in the range of $5-6 Bn.

PayNearby

Kicking off its IPO preparations, cofounder and CEO Bajaj shared in August 2025 that PayNearby is eyeing a FY27 listing. The company is also finalising a merchant banker as it looks to file its DRHP with the SEBI soon.

PayU India

Notably, a few months later in September, reports once again surfaced that the fintech major was looking to raise $250 Mn to $300 Mn in a pre-IPO round to broaden its investor base, test demand, and set a benchmark valuation for the listing.

Practo

The health tech startup has raised nearly $230 Mn in funding to date from the likes of Tencent, Peak XV Partners (then Sequoia Capital), Z47 Partners (erstwhile Matrix Partners India), Sofina, among others. 

Practo was initially planning to list on the Indian bourses in 2026 but has now moved the IPO timeline to 2027. Rebel Foods

The startup has so far amassed over $563 Mn in funding from the likes of Coatue Management, Lightbox, Peak XV Partners, and Temasek. The startup was last pegged at $1.4 Bn during its last $25 Mn fundraise from Qatar Investment Authority in April 2025. 

The company’s IPO plans first came to light in October 2024 after reports surfaced that Rebel Foods was looking to list on the bourses in the next 18 months (April 2026). However, the company is yet to even file its DRHP. 

However, in a major top-level rejig in July 2025, the company’s cofounder and India CEO Ankush Grover was appointed as global CEO, while incumbent Jaydeep Barman was elevated to the role of chairman and group CEO.

On the financial front, the unicorn’s net losses shrank 12% to ₹336.6 Cr in FY25 from ₹380.3 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenues grew 14% to ₹1,617.4 Cr from ₹1,420.2 Cr in FY24.

Servify

Servify was previously looking to list on the exchanges by Q1 2026, but the plan looks far-fetched as the company is yet to even file its draft IPO papers with the markets regulator. 

Meanwhile, Servify saw hefty improvement on the financial front in FY24 as loss shrank 59% YoY to ₹93.81 Cr. This came largely on the back of operating revenue increasing 23% YoY to ₹754 Cr in the fiscal under review. 

Spinny

Founded in 2015 by Niraj Singh, Mohit Gupta, and Ganesh Pawar, Spinny operates a full-stack marketplace that enables users to buy and sell certified used cars. Unlike aggregators, the platform owns the inventory and refurbishes cars in-house.

On the financial front, Spinny’s net loss declined 28% to ₹423.8 Cr in FY25 from ₹590.3 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue rose 25% to ₹4,656.1 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹3,730 Cr in FY24.

Square Yards

If the IPO materialises, Square Yards will be among a handful of Indian startups where founders will continue to hold more than 50% stake. 

On the financial front, the proptech startup clocked an operating revenue of ₹2,086 Cr in FY26 on a gross profit of ₹476 Cr.

Udaan

It also has a fintech platform called udaanCapital, which offers financial services to small businesses and helps them with their working capital requirements. 

Backed by marquee names such as Lightspeed, DST Global, Altimeter Capital and Tencent, Udaan has raised more than $2.17 Bn in funding to date.

Wonderchef

The startup sells its offerings via its own website, ecommerce platforms as well as its own exclusive business outlets (EBOs). Backed by the likes of Sixth Sense Ventures, Amicus Capital, Godrej Family Office, Malpani Group, among others, the brand has raised more than $30 Mn in funding to date.

Zypp Electric

Founded in 2017 by Akash Gupta and Tushar Mehta, Zypp offers EV-based mobility solutions for delivery workers. Besides the core EV leasing business, it also operates EV battery swapping, maintenance and servicing infrastructure.

It also runs an advertising business and has developed a fleet management software platform, called Fleekies.ai.

Ahead of the listing, Zypp Electric is looking to raise a pre-IPO round in the range of $40-50 Mn from private equity firms and impact-focused funds. 

On the financial front, Zypp Electric’s revenue from operations zoomed 49% to ₹438 Cr in FY25 from ₹293 Cr in the previous year. Meanwhile, net loss widened 20.1% to ₹107.5 Cr from ₹89.5 Cr in FY24.

item.title: Budget 2027: Industry Body BWA Seeks Tax Relief For Crypto Startups
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Industry body Bharat Web3 Association (BWA) has submitted its recommendations to the finance ministry ahead of the upcoming Union Budget…
item.content:encoded:
Industry body Bharat Web3 Association (BWA) has submitted its recommendations to the finance ministry ahead of the upcoming Union Budget 2027. It has sought a fairer taxation framework and greater regulatory certainty for the Indian cryptocurrency sector.

“The BWA submission focused on the need for a fair, balanced and effective taxation framework that encourages compliance, strengthens investor protection, enhances tax revenues and supports the growth of India’s domestic Web3 ecosystem,” said the industry body in a post on X.

BWA urged the ministry to consider the following recommendations for the Indian virtual digital asset (VDA) sector while drafting Budget 2027:

  • Level the playing field by clarifying and strengthening the applicability of Indian tax provisions, particularly TDS obligations, to offshore VDA platforms serving Indian users
  • Reconsider the existing 1% TDS, permit set-off and carry-forward of losses, and review the 30% tax rate (on profits from sale of cryptos) to encourage greater user participation
  • Improve the enforcement of registration and reporting obligations 
  • Ensure offshore entities serving Indian users are subject to appropriate Indian legal and regulatory requirements
  • Provide regulatory clarity for FIU-registered crypto exchanges, which seek access to global liquidity through offshore exchanges

BWA also noted that clear and consistent guidelines for cryptocurrencies would provide much-needed certainty to compliant Indian platforms and strengthen the domestic ecosystem. 

“A framework that encourages activity within compliant Indian platforms can strengthen oversight, improve tax compliance and support innovation and investment in India,” added BWA.

This comes as the Indian cryptocurrency sector has been constantly appealing to the Centre to reduce the TDS on VDAs for the last four years. They have also been seeking tax breaks for the development of blockchain security infrastructure as well as tax holidays for early-stage Web3 platforms. 

However, the finance ministry has largely unheeded these demands and has opted for a heavy-taxation approach towards crypto platforms. Meanwhile, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) remains a steadfast opponent of digital currencies. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra last year even said that cryptocurrencies could potentially affect the country’s financial stability. 

A Parliamentary standing committee on finance recently also termed the asset class as “high risk” citing rampant money laundering, trafficking, radicalisation and suspicious crypto transactions.

The recommendations also come as the Indian crypto ecosystem continues to be under strain. Over the past few months, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) has also intensified scrutiny of crypto-related financial flows and raided multiple crypto exchanges over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions.

Making matters worse has been the recent spate of delays and disruptions in withdrawals at major crypto exchanges including Coinbase India, CoinDCX and Zebpay. 

While the three platforms have cited issues at banking partners for the disruption, industry insiders pointed to heightened scrutiny of intermediaries handling crypto-related financial flows as a possible source of pressure on banking and liquidity arrangements. 

As if this was not enough, many crypto platforms have been hit by data breaches and hacks amid a surge in AI-assisted cyberattacks.

item.title: Atomberg & Voltas Execute JV Agreement To Build AC Compressors
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: IPO-bound consumer appliances startup Atomberg has executed a joint venture (JV) agreement with Tata-owned Voltas to manufacture compressors for room…
item.content:encoded:
IPO-bound consumer appliances startup Atomberg has executed a joint venture (JV) agreement with Tata-owned Voltas to manufacture compressors for room air conditioners (ACs) and other allied parts in India.

In a statement, Voltas said that Atomberg Innovation Private Limited’s (AIPL) wholly-owned subsidiary Atomberg Airtech Private Limited (AAPL) will be designated as the JV entity. 

Under the agreement, Voltas will acquire a 50% equity stake in AAPL from AIPL upon closing the transaction. Both Voltas and AIPL have committed to infuse up to ₹100 Cr each in tranches in the JV. 

The Joint Venture will be held on an equal shareholding basis, i.e. Voltas – 50% and AIPL 50%. The maximum funding commitment by each party to the Joint Venture will be ₹100 crores, to be infused in tranches from time to time on such terms as may be decided by the board of the joint venture entity,” said Voltas in a filing with the exchanges.

Interestingly, Voltas will have the right to nominate four directors to the board of AAPL while Atomberg will be able to nominate one director. Voltas will also have the right to control the composition of AAPL’s board, said the Tata-owned brand in a statement. 

Consequently, AAPL will become a subsidiary of Voltas upon completion of the transaction. The name of AAPL is proposed to be changed following the closing of the transaction, added Voltas.

The completion of the transaction remains subject to the fulfilment of conditions specified in the JV agreement, added Voltas. 

Atomberg and Voltas had earlier signed a binding term sheet to form a JV in the AC manufacturing space back in August. The update has now revealed further details around the JV entity including its governance and corporate structure. 

At the time, Voltas had further committed to being an anchor customer of the JV in order to provide a “stable demand base,” while noting that it would not be an exclusive arrangement and the JV would still be able to supply compressors to other customers. 

Founded in 2012 by IIT Bombay alumni Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg initially operated on a B2B model and sold energy-efficient BLDC fans. It entered the consumer market in 2016. 

Today, it sells a range of appliances such as mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. 

It entered the B2B manufacturing business via AIPL in March this year to build motors and controllers for home appliances including refrigerators and washing machines as well as ACs. 

The move to diversify its revenue stream comes ahead of the company’s planned IPO. In August, it filed its DRHP with SEBI, proposing to raise up to ₹450 Cr via a fresh issue of shares. Investors also plan to sell up to 7.65 Cr equity shares through an offer-for-sale (OFS) component.

item.title: Stalled Withdrawals, Millions Stolen: Inside India’s Crypto Exchange Troubles
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: India’s cryptocurrency exchanges are facing turbulence on multiple fronts, with banking disruptions, regulatory scrutiny, and cybersecurity incidents exposing vulnerabilities across…
item.content:encoded:
India’s cryptocurrency exchanges are facing turbulence on multiple fronts, with banking disruptions, regulatory scrutiny, and cybersecurity incidents exposing vulnerabilities across the industry.

Over the past few weeks, Coinbase, CoinDCX, and ZebPay have reported delays or disruptions in INR withdrawals, each citing issues at banking partners. Separately, Unocoin disclosed estimated cryptocurrency losses of $0.2 Mn following a security breach, while CoinDCX reported a loss of 15.99 Mn USDT (Tether), worth approximately $16 Mn, from retired wallet infrastructure in October. 

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has also intensified scrutiny of crypto-related financial flows, searching premises linked to CoinDCX and Delta Exchange in November over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions.

These developments expose different weaknesses across banking access, liquidity arrangements, and wallet security.

Banking Channels Under Strain

Coinbase India reported a banking partner outage on November 9 that disrupted its regular INR withdrawal facility. By November 20, it was processing pending withdrawals in batches through an alternative route, asking customers to contact support for transfers expected to take 48-72 hours.

CoinDCX, meanwhile, warned users on November 19 that INR withdrawals were taking longer than usual because of processing changes at its banking partners. It initially said most withdrawals were being completed within four to six hours.

Yesterday, the exchange said it processed 90% of withdrawal requests in under 90 minutes over the preceding 20 hours, with an average processing time of 68 minutes. It attributed the delays to ongoing system upgrades at banks but did not specify when real-time withdrawals would resume.

ZebPay also reported INR withdrawal delays following a technical disruption at its banking partner. None of the three exchanges has identified the banks involved or confirmed whether the disruptions are connected.

The disruptions come amid wider changes to banking infrastructure. Inc42 reported that Yes Bank’s upgrades to strengthen defences against AI-driven cyberattacks were disrupting payment service providers, with changes to its banking APIs delaying payment processing and settlements, according to industry sources.

Industry participants Inc42 spoke to pointed to heightened scrutiny of intermediaries handling crypto-related financial flows as a possible source of pressure on banking and liquidity arrangements. 

Scrutiny Of Liquidity Channels

In June, the ED searched six premises in Bengaluru linked to five platforms – Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money, and Onmeta – over alleged unauthorised cross-border transfers using virtual digital assets (VDAs).

The agency alleged that the entities facilitated international money transfers through cryptocurrencies and stablecoins without the necessary authorisations under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA).

In November, the ED searched premises linked to CoinDCX and Delta Exchange over alleged unauthorised cross-border financial transactions involving crypto derivatives and real-world asset tokens. The agency alleged that the platforms used stablecoins to route transactions through overseas crypto platforms. 

The action had repercussions for domestic liquidity. Following the searches, market makers and liquidity providers reportedly pulled back from sourcing USDT overseas, tightening domestic supply. The stablecoin’s premium on Indian platforms subsequently rose above 8.5%, compared with its usual 3-4% range.

The ED’s scrutiny continued in November, when it searched premises linked to CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India over alleged unauthorised cross-border financial transactions involving crypto derivatives and real-world asset tokens. The watchdog alleged routing of customer transactions through overseas platforms using stablecoins. These remain allegations under investigation.

Exchanges rely on market makers and liquidity providers to facilitate trading. An industry executive familiar with crypto liquidity operations told Inc42 that enforcement action against intermediaries and heightened banking scrutiny are making it harder for exchanges to source liquidity through established channels.

Dependence on external providers was also evident in October, when CoinDCX placed its futures platform in reduce-only mode, allowing users to reduce or close positions while restricting new ones. The exchange cited developments affecting a global liquidity provider, later identified as Binance.

Binance separately disclosed an October 29 cyberattack affecting approximately $6.3 Bn in digital assets. The exchange said it had replenished 98% of the impacted tokens by October 31.

The Binance breach highlights the security risks facing exchanges globally. In India, recent incidents at Unocoin and CoinDCX have exposed weaknesses in backup-key management and retired wallet infrastructure.

Wallet Controls Under Test

Unocoin detected suspicious activity on November 6 and suspended all services on November 9 while investigating a compromise of its infrastructure.

In a November 14 update, the exchange said three operational hot wallets had been compromised, resulting in estimated cryptocurrency losses of $0.2 Mn. Hot wallets remain connected to the internet to facilitate transactions, unlike cold wallets, which keep signing keys offline.

Unocoin said the unauthorised transactions used compromised backup signing keys associated with its multisignature wallets. It committed to covering the identified loss from its own resources without deducting it from customer balances.

It also flagged potential exposure of customer information, including email addresses, residential addresses, encrypted passwords, account balances, and KYC-related details. 

The disclosure followed CoinDCX’s October loss from wallet infrastructure retired after its July 2025 security breach.

The two incidents highlight risks extending beyond active trading systems to backup keys, retired infrastructure, and the processes used to move funds between wallets.

AI Broadens Cyber Threats

Preetam Rao, cofounder and CEO of blockchain security firm QuillAudits, said employees and third-party technology providers are increasingly becoming entry points for attackers.

“The biggest risk today is an engineer’s laptop,” Rao said, citing fake freelance job offers, malicious software, and compromised developer tools used to access organisational systems.

Separately, CERT-In issued a November 4 advisory warning of AI-assisted attacks targeting NBFCs, fintech companies, payment aggregators, payment service providers, and cryptocurrency exchanges.

The agency identified a threat actor designated CRAFTY FALCON, which it said used machine intelligence to identify weaknesses and exploit payment and disbursement APIs to execute unauthorised transfers.

In a fresh advisory on November 20, CERT-In also flagged unauthorised transactions involving service providers supporting government-linked payments and vendor payouts. Attackers manipulated business records and approval processes to move funds through legitimate payment systems.

AI-assisted attacks are also widening the challenge for exchanges, putting pressure on them to strengthen defences beyond wallet security.

Ritesh Bhatia, a cybersecurity expert and ransomware negotiator, said AI is increasing the speed and scale at which attackers could identify vulnerabilities.

“The vulnerabilities which weren’t seen by the human mind are now being seen by AI” he said.

Bhatia argued that organisations need stronger security resources and defensive use of AI to identify weaknesses. He also stressed the importance of incident response and disaster recovery, given the difficulty of preventing every attack.

For crypto exchanges, losses can be particularly difficult to contain because blockchain transfers generally cannot be reversed unilaterally. Rao called for stronger controls over private keys, employee devices, wallet access, and third-party infrastructure.

Stronger Rules And Safeguards

The recent disruptions have sharpened the case for clearer rules on how India’s crypto exchanges hold customer assets, manage operational risks, and communicate when things go wrong.

Rao recommended keeping the bulk of customer assets in cold storage, setting transaction limits, and requiring independent approvals for sensitive wallet transfers. He also called for backup keys and recovery passphrases to be stored offline.

Such safeguards need to cover the entire custody system, including backup-key access and retired wallets that continue to receive deposits – weaknesses exposed by the Unocoin and CoinDCX incidents. 

Rao pointed to Hong Kong and Japan as examples of jurisdictions with more prescriptive custody requirements. Hong Kong requires licensed virtual asset trading platforms to keep 98% of customer crypto assets in cold storage, while Japan requires at least 95% to be managed offline.

India’s crypto-specific framework primarily focuses on anti-money laundering compliance. A dedicated framework could establish consistent custody standards, independent audit requirements, customer notification timelines, and mechanisms for addressing losses and complaints.

Clearer rules could also give banks, payment providers, and institutional liquidity partners greater certainty about working with exchanges, the industry executive quoted earlier said.

For exchanges, the immediate task is to diversify banking and liquidity partners, strengthen source-of-funds checks, and tighten security controls. Regulation could set a common minimum standard, but exchanges remain responsible for ensuring those safeguards work when customers need to withdraw money or attackers find a way in.

item.title: Swish FY26: Revenue Surges Close To ₹50 Cr While Loss Widens To ₹91 Cr
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Quick food delivery startup Swish clocked in a revenue of over ₹50 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26). However,…
item.content:encoded:
Quick food delivery startup Swish clocked in a revenue of over ₹50 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26). However, heavy expenses pushed the Bengaluru-based startup deep into the red. 

Swish’s operating revenue for the fiscal jumped over 10X YoY to ₹47.6 Cr, while its net loss surged close to 4X to ₹91.1 Cr during the year.

Notably, Swish’s FY25 financial statements cover only the period between July 8, 2024, and March 31, 2025, following its incorporation in July 2024. Therefore, the year-on-year growth figures are based on a shorter operating period and are not directly comparable with a full-year performance.

The startup’s total income, including other income, rose to ₹53.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹4.2 Cr in FY25. Meanwhile, its total expenses surged more than 5X to ₹144.8 Cr, significantly outpacing revenue growth.

Founded in 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja and Saran S, Swish operates a vertically integrated quick food delivery model, with the startup owning and managing its neighbourhood kitchens, technology and last-mile delivery operations. 

Its kitchens typically serve customers within a one-kilometre radius, with the platform promising food deliveries in around 10-15 minutes.

Unlike the asset-light aggregator model followed by Swiggy and Zomato, Swish operates its own kitchens, with dedicated preparation, cooking and assembly stations. 

The startup has expanded its presence across Bengaluru, Gurugram, Noida, Delhi and Ghaziabad, covering nearly 50 pincodes.

In September 2026, Swish raised $24 Mn (around ₹228 Cr) in a funding round led by Bertelsmann India Investments, with participation from existing investors Accel, Bain Capital Ventures and Hara Global. 

The startup said it would use the proceeds to expand its kitchen network, enter new cities and strengthen its supply chain infrastructure. It is targeting a network of more than 1,000 kitchens over the next five years. Prior to that it also raised $38 Mn in March 2026.

The startup has also been experimenting with new delivery formats. 

In October 2026, it began piloting Swish Go, a feature that allows customers to order food from third-party restaurants and cloud kitchens, marking a departure from its core kitchen-led model. The service is being tested in select Bengaluru pincodes and is positioned around affordable food delivery without packaging and platform fees.

Swish’s Expenses Surge 5X

Swish’s employee benefit expenses emerged as its largest expense head, rising over 5X to ₹55.71 Cr in FY26 from ₹10.37 Cr in FY25. Cost of goods sold jumped 586% to ₹39.48 Cr, while other expenses surged 565% to ₹44.39 Cr during the year.

The widening losses come amid increased scrutiny over the economics of ultra-fast food delivery. Several players, including Swiggy, have recalibrated their bets in the segment, with the latter shutting down its standalone 10-minute food delivery app SNACC earlier this year amid profitability concerns. 

Zing has also moved away from the model, citing weaker-than-expected demand and high operating costs.

item.title: DGGI Probes ₹1 Lakh Cr China-Linked Gaming Transactions
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: The Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI) conducted searches across Vijayawada and Hyderabad’s Banjara Hills as part of an investigation…
item.content:encoded:
The Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI) conducted searches across Vijayawada and Hyderabad’s Banjara Hills as part of an investigation into around ₹1 Lakh Cr of online gaming transactions suspected to be linked to China. 

Hyderabad-based firms allegedly worked with Chinese entities to operate four gaming platforms – superwinner, bigrummywinner, bigluckywinner, and rummyruler – and the associated Android platforms, according to the agency. 

The agency is investigating the firms’ promoters’ alleged meeting with a Chinese intermediary in 2023 to set up domestic payment gateway services, while a China-based digital marketing team drove user acquisition. This helped siphon money to China via crypto. 

It is also alleged that payment aggregators used settlement accounts under dummy merchants, while certain intermediaries onboarded dummy merchants to boost platform fees, floating income, and turnover. 

The scheme is suspected to also involve potential use of cryptocurrencies such as USDT and suspected syndicate members in Dubai and Singapore. 

The DGGI team recorded the statement of Gali Kiran Kumar, and are also looking into the involvement of Satyanarayana Itakari, chairman and MD of First Finance Credit Cooperative Society. For context, the same entity was linked to the Karnataka Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation scam where funds intended for the welfare of tribal communities were siphoned and routed to bogus accounts. 

It won’t be unfair to say that illicit offshore gaming operators have picked up operations across India following a ban on online real money gaming. Head Digital Works, operator of A23 Rummy, alleged that legitimate businesses are suffering while illegitimate operators are booming. The remarks were highlighted before a Supreme Court bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant. 

Head Digital Works was seeking an early hearing around the real money gaming ban in a challenge brought by several gaming operators including Clubboom11 Sports & Entertainment (Boom11) and Bagheera Carrom. The Supreme Court has agreed to hear their plea on December 2.

The ban had brought the industry to a near standstill, triggering mass layoffs and even shutdowns. Gaming startup Zupee constitutes one such example. It had claimed it was pivoting to AI but appears to have laid off its entire workforce and nearly wound up operations. 

Another prominent player in hot water after the regulatory crackdown is Gamekraft, which is also under scrutiny from the Enforcement Directorate (ED) over alleged money laundering. In total, the ED has attached, frozen, or seized assets worth around ₹2,843 Cr as part of its investigation.

item.title: New-Age Tech Stocks Miss Market Rally This Week, Paytm Sheds 10.8%
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: New-age tech stocks largely missed the rally in Indian equities this week, with only 22 of the 69 stocks under…
item.content:encoded:
New-age tech stocks largely missed the rally in Indian equities this week, with only 22 of the 69 stocks under Inc42’s coverage ending higher.
Zelio E-Mobility led the gainers with a 19.6% rise, followed by Veefin at 18.8% and Yatra at 14%. Gains across the 22 stocks ranged from 0.2% to 19.6%.

Nine stocks – Tonbo, Shadowfax, Honasa, Meesho, Groww, Nykaa, Ather, BlackBuck and Nazara – touched fresh 52-week highs this week.

Meanwhile, 47 new-age tech stocks ended the week in the red. Zappfresh recorded the steepest decline at 29.6%, followed by TAC Infosec at 22.6%, and E2E Networks at 15.2%.

Shiprocket shed 14.2%, while Aye Finance fell 12.4%. Zaggle Prepaid Ocean Services declined 11.6%, followed by Paytm at 10.8%. FirstCry, DroneAcharya, TAC Infosec, and Zappfresh touched fresh lows.

The combined market capitalisation of the 69 stocks remained nearly flat at $176.9 Bn, down about $100 Mn from $177 Bn the previous week.

Here are the key developments at listed new-age tech companies this week:

Urban Company Raises ₹2,500 Cr: The home services marketplace raised ₹2,500 Cr through a QIP, attracting bids worth more than ₹15,000 Cr from over 60 institutional investors. It allotted 16.02 Cr shares at ₹156 apiece, a 3.1% discount to the floor price of ₹161.03. The company plans to deploy ₹600 Cr towards InstaHelp over FY27-FY29, alongside investments in technology, marketing, and its Native product business.

PB Fintech Cofounder Steps Back: Cofounder Alok Bansal will step down from his executive responsibilities when his term expires on March 31, 2027. He will transition to a non-executive director role from April 1. Bansal cofounded Policybazaar with Yashish Dahiya in 2008.

Aye Finance Plans Debt Raise: The NBFC approved raising up to ₹325 Cr through three series of secured, listed non-convertible debentures (NCDs) via private placement, including a greenshoe option of ₹75 Cr. The NCDs will be listed on BSE’s Wholesale Debt Market segment, with allotment proposed for November 25.

PB Fintech Liquidates Subsidiary: The Policybazaar parent liquidated its Abu Dhabi-based step-down subsidiary, Zphin Computer Systems and Software Designing-Sole Proprietorship, effective November 18. Its net worth stood at AED 73,441 (₹18.8 Lakh), equivalent to 0.003% of PB Fintech’s net worth.

Ribbit Capital Trims Groww Stake: The investor sold a 1.4% stake in Groww for ₹1,905.3 Cr through multiple block deals, offloading 8.7 Cr shares at ₹219 apiece. Buyers included funds affiliated with BlackRock and Fidelity, Societe Generale, and domestic mutual funds.

Tonbo Bags Defence Order: The defence tech company secured a ₹35.6 Cr order from the Ministry of Defence to supply clip-on thermal weapon sights for assault rifles and associated support equipment. The contract includes an option clause and a repeat-order clause, each permitting additional orders of up to 50% of the original quantity at the ministry’s discretion.

Awfis Appoints New CBO: The company appointed Kumar Alok Gupta as chief business officer to oversee demand and supply initiatives across its managed office and coworking businesses. Gupta has over 24 years of commercial real estate experience and previously served as MD at Cushman & Wakefield.
Now, let’s take a look at the performance of the broader market this week.

Benchmarks Extend Winning Streak

Indian equities rose for a fourth consecutive week, with the Nifty 50 gaining 2.6% to close at 25,800.60 and the Sensex advancing 2.9% to 83,919.71.
The rally was narrower beyond the benchmarks. The Nifty Midcap 100 edged up 0.2%, while the Nifty Smallcap 100 declined 1.1%.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) bought a net ₹32,600 Cr worth of equities across the five sessions, marking their fourth consecutive week of net buying. Domestic institutional investors (DIIs) sold a net ₹12,700 Cr, leaving combined net inflows of ₹19,900 Cr.

According to Pabitro Mukherjee, deputy vice president of research at Bajaj Broking, FII net purchases have reached around ₹1.12 Lakh Cr in November, compared with net selling of ₹45,162 Cr in October. DII selling continued for a third consecutive week, although the pace moderated.
Geojit Investments’ head of research Vinod Nair attributed the market’s resilience to foreign inflows into large-cap stocks, particularly banks, and easing concerns over crude oil prices and inflation. He also pointed to a rotation of global capital away from crowded AI trades, with Indian equities outperforming other Asian markets amid a broader technology sell-off.

Next week, investors will track NSE’s November monthly derivatives expiry on Monday, November 23, ahead of the trading holiday for Guru Nanak Jayanti on Tuesday, November 24.

Mukherjee flagged rising FII short positions in index futures despite continued cash-market buying. Crude oil prices, developments in West Asia, upcoming domestic GDP data, and the RBI policy decision will also influence sentiment.

Nair said earnings and interest rates would remain key drivers, with the possibility of a December rate hike adding uncertainty. He nevertheless maintained a constructive longer-term outlook, citing earnings visibility and continued foreign interest in large-cap stocks.

Now, let’s take a detailed look at the performance of Zelio E-Mobility and Paytm this week.

Zelio Leads Weekly Gains

Shares of Zelio E-Mobility rose 19.6% this week to close at ₹1,348.35 yesterday. The gains followed the electric two-wheeler maker’s H1 FY27 results and updates on its fundraising and manufacturing expansion.

The company received in-principle approval from BSE for a proposed preferential issue of 9.73 Lakh equity shares to non-promoters and 9.96 Lakh convertible warrants to promoters, at a minimum issue price of ₹853 apiece. The proposed issue could raise around ₹168 Cr, subject to subscription and completion of the required process.

Zelio also commenced commercial production at its fourth manufacturing facility in Patan, Hisar, on October 28. The plant has an annual production capacity of 3.12 Lakh units.

For H1 FY27, the company reported consolidated net profit of ₹31.4 Cr, up 164.3%, while operating revenue increased 120% to ₹296.7 Cr. EBITDA stood at ₹40.5 Cr, with its margin expanding to 13.6% from around 12% a year earlier. Its first-half operating revenue approached the ₹313.7 Cr reported for FY26, while net profit exceeded the previous full-year figure of ₹28.4 Cr.

Paytm Falls On MDR Uncertainty

Paytm shares declined 10.8% this week amid uncertainty over the rollout of merchant discount rate (MDR) charges on select UPI transactions. The stock closed at ₹1,735 on the BSE yesterday. MDR is the fee merchants pay for processing payments. The proposed framework would levy a 0.4% charge on eligible person-to-merchant UPI transactions above ₹2,000.

The rollout was initially scheduled for October 15 before being deferred until after Diwali. This week, Financial Express reported that implementation could slip beyond the 2027 state elections, with the government, RBI, and National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) yet to agree on a date.

A further delay would push back a potential transaction-fee revenue stream for Paytm and other participants in the UPI ecosystem. Other fintech stocks also declined. Pine Labs fell 9.4% during the week, while MobiKwik shed 6.6%.

During the week, Paytm’s board also approved investing up to ₹200 Cr through its Singapore subsidiary in Funding Societies’ group companies, including ₹162 Cr for a 19.1% stake in payments firm CardUp.

On the financial front, Paytm reported net profit of ₹225 Cr in Q2 FY27, more than 10 times the year-ago figure, while revenue rose 28% YoY to ₹2,648 Cr.

item.title: Exclusive: Bewakoof Cofounder Prabhkiran Singh Launches AI Shopping Assistant Save8
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: Bewakoof cofounder and former CEO Prabhkiran Singh has launched Save8, an AI-powered shopping assistant that helps consumers compare prices and…
item.content:encoded:
Bewakoof cofounder and former CEO Prabhkiran Singh has launched Save8, an AI-powered shopping assistant that helps consumers compare prices and offers across ecommerce and quick commerce platforms.

The venture comes months after Singh stepped down from Bewakoof, the D2C fashion brand he led for nearly 14 years.

Singh is also looking to raise external capital for Save8 and has held talks with investors, including All In Capital, sources told Inc42. The proposed funding amount and the final investor lineup could not be ascertained.

Questions sent to Singh about Save8’s launch, business model, and fundraising plans remained unanswered till the time of publication.

According to its website, Save8 aggregates prices and offers across more than 1,000 online stores. It compares product prices alongside coupons, cashback, discounted gift cards, and bank offers to help shoppers identify potential savings.

How Does Save8 Work?

Users can compare offers by pasting a product link into Save8’s website, adding ‘save8.ai/’ before the product URL in their browser’s address bar, or sending the link to the Save8 app through a shopping app’s share menu.

The platform lists Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Zepto, Blinkit, and Swiggy Instamart among the services it covers. Its comparison tools aim to help users assess purchase costs after accounting for available discounts and payment offers. 

Save8 is available through its website and mobile applications. Its Google Play listing says it displays available bank and payment offers but does not automatically apply them.

Save8 operates under ThousandX Ventures LLP, according to its terms of service. Besides its deal-finding tools, Save8 facilitates the purchase of digital gift cards issued by brands or their authorised partners.

Singh’s Return To Entrepreneurship

Singh cofounded Bewakoof in 2012. In February this year, he announced plans to step down as CEO at the end of March, citing personal priorities, including health and family.

His departure ended a nearly 14-year stint at the company. Aditya Birla Group’s digital-first venture TMRW invested ₹200 Cr to acquire a majority stake in Bewakoof, with the transaction completed in February 2023. 

During Singh’s tenure, Bewakoof built a youth-focused fashion business catering to millennials and Gen Z shoppers, expanding beyond its own D2C platform into online marketplaces and offline retail.

With Save8, Singh is moving from selling consumer products to helping shoppers compare where and how to buy them.

item.title: IIT Delhi Alumnus’ Startup Sues Apple For ₹1,500 Cr Over NameDrop Patent Infringement
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: What happens when two iPhones are brought close together? Users get to exchange contact details without typing or scanning a…
item.content:encoded:
What happens when two iPhones are brought close together? Users get to exchange contact details without typing or scanning a QR code with NameDrop. 

For GG Technologies, a startup founded by IIT Delhi alumnus Gaurav Goel in 2018, this feature is at the heart of a patent dispute which sees it lock horns with the tech giant Apple. 

GG, the parent company of contact-sharing app StayTouch, claims it developed and patented the underlying technology years before Apple introduced NameDrop in 2023. It has now approached the Bombay High Court (HC), alleging that the feature infringes its Indian patent. The startup has moved the court seeking directions that mandate Apple to disable NameDrop in India while the case is heard. 

Separately, GG Technologies is seeking ₹1,500 Cr in damages.

As per its 781-page plaint and accompanying documents, accessed by Inc42, the startup has asked the court to direct Apple to switch off NameDrop in India, including through a software update, “to the extent technically feasible”. Apple could continue selling its devices without the disputed feature.

A Patent Versus An Ecosystem

GG argues that Apple has a structural advantage because NameDrop is built into compatible devices, while StayTouch requires a separate app download. The startup claims this has hurt its ability to secure commercial partnerships, with prospective partners already being offered similar functionality by Apple. 

GG cited Apple’s annual India sales crossing $10 Bn to illustrate its distribution scale, clarifying that this is not an estimate of NameDrop revenue. 

A chartered accountant’s certificate puts GG’s technical development and marketing expenditure between 2019 and 2025 at $2.75 Mn.

The startup has sought ₹1,500 Cr in damages, calling it a conservative estimate. It says the final calculation would depend on device and revenue information held by Apple. However, the plaint does not provide an independent calculation supporting the claim.

Inc42 has reached out to Apple for a response.

How Similar Are The Two Technologies?

The dispute centres on Indian Patent No. 546169, titled ‘Method and System for Proximity-Based Contact Transfer’, granted to GG on July 27, 2024. Its patent filings began in May 2019, while Apple announced NameDrop in June 2023.

The patent describes a system that detects nearby devices, exchanges identifying information and allows users to accept or decline contact transfers. It also provides for a central server to maintain contact profiles and synchronise changes.

GG alleges that NameDrop follows a similar process, citing proximity-based discovery, device identification, user consent and selective sharing. It also argues that Apple’s iCloud infrastructure performs the central-server function described in the patent.

Two expert reports commissioned by GG identify substantial technical similarities. However, neither expert had access to Apple’s source code. The assessments rely on publicly available information and are not court-appointed findings. Therefore, Apple could contest whether NameDrop uses the same identifiers, server architecture or sequence of operations.

GG launched StayTouch’s global beta in July 2019 and showcased the product at Web Summit that year and CES in January 2020. It says it began exploring commercial partnerships in 2024 and commissioned technical assessments of NameDrop in February 2026.

What Happens Next?

GG’s legal action against Apple extends beyond India. It filed a patent infringement suit in the US in April 2026, which has been stayed since September pending a separate US International Trade Commission (USITC) investigation. The commission instituted the investigation in August. A favourable ruling could restrict imports of infringing devices into the US.

GG filed another US patent infringement suit against Apple on November 3, citing a separate patent.

“When I conceived StayTouch in 2018, the idea was simple: make sharing contact information easier, faster and more intuitive,” Goel said.

The Bombay High Court proceedings are ongoing. GG told Inc42 that the first hearing is yet to be scheduled.

item.title: Sarvam’s Token Factory Raises India’s AI Inference Stakes
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: Sarvam AI’s latest announcement of its Token Factory has brought a new layer of India’s artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure ecosystem…
item.content:encoded:
Sarvam AI’s latest announcement of its Token Factory has brought a new layer of India’s artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure ecosystem into focus. The Bengaluru-based startup on November 16 launched a commercial platform that allows developers and enterprises to access multiple AI models through its computing infrastructure.

The launch comes as Indian companies look to capitalise on the growing demand for AI inference, the process through which trained models generate responses to user prompts. While much of the country’s AI infrastructure investments have so far gone into setting up data centres and procuring GPUs, the growing adoption of AI applications is creating demand for infrastructure that can efficiently serve models at scale.

A token factory allows developers and enterprises to access multiple AI models through a common API, without having to procure GPUs, deploy models or manage the underlying infrastructure. It handles model hosting, computing resources and inference optimisation, charging customers for the input and output tokens they consume rather than for GPU capacity or server time.

Unlike GPU-as-a-service providers and neoclouds, which primarily offer the infrastructure on which customers run their own workloads, a token factory sits a layer above, using owned or leased GPU capacity to serve inference requests through APIs. This reduces the operational burden on customers and allows them to switch between models based on their requirements.

Sarvam is not alone in this pursuit. Larsen & Toubro (L&T), E2E Networks through its Jarvislabs business, and AI security startup Mirror Security are among the other players building offerings around token-based inference. The emerging category also has global precedents, with companies such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, DeepInfra, and Nebius operating similar platforms.

Sarvam’s Token Factory and The Sovereignty Debate

Sarvam’s Token Factory hosts the company’s proprietary Sarvam 105B model alongside open-weight models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3 and Google’s Gemma 4 31B. 

The billing is in Indian rupee. Sarvam has priced its Token Factory on a pay-per-token basis, with separate rates for input, cached input, and output tokens. Its flagship Sarvam 105B model is priced at an introductory ₹10 per Mn input tokens and ₹25 per Mn output tokens. For other models, prices range from ₹14 (per million input tokens) to ₹950 (per Mn output tokens). 

The platform has been serving more than 450 Bn tokens daily through DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, highlighting the scale of demand for inference services, the company said in its blog. 

However, the launch of the token factory has also brought up two questions for Sarvam from the ecosystem: why a beneficiary of the government’s IndiaAI Mission, which is aimed at developing indigenous AI capabilities, is hosting Chinese-developed models, and whether GPUs subsidised under the mission are powering the service.

The company was selected under the mission to develop homegrown foundation models and received access to 4,096 Nvidia H100 GPUs. The six-month computing allocation was worth around ₹247 Cr, including a government subsidy of ₹98.68 Cr. 

Sarvam, however, clarified that its Token Factory does not use GPU capacity subsidised under the IndiaAI Mission. Instead, it runs on GPUs privately procured by the company. It also said that its access to the government-supported GPU capacity ended in March 2026. The company added that there were no commercial arrangements involving licensing fees, data sharing or royalties with the developers of the hosted models. These are open-weight models that can be downloaded and deployed on privately owned infrastructure.

The company has not responded to Inc42’s questionnaire around this. 

“Token Factory gives Sarvam a reason to keep its B200 cluster busy between training runs, and income that lets the company breathe while its trillion-parameter model is built,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst of Greyhound Research, told Inc42. “Sarvam’s product team has reason to feel confident and exposed at once. Its founders should show by the end of 2027 that customers who arrived for DeepSeek stayed for Sarvam.”

The Data Question And The Economic Model 

Running a token factory on its own GPUs also means Sarvam carries the cost of idle capacity. On the serverless tier, customers pay only for the tokens they use, while Sarvam pays for its B200 cluster whether it is busy or not. That makes utilisation, rather than headline volume, the number that decides whether the service makes money.

The company added that 95.7% of the prompt tokens it serves on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash come from cache, which it bills at ₹0.25 per Mn tokens against ₹14 per Mn for fresh input. At those rates, 450 Bn prompt tokens a day would bring in about ₹13.8 Cr a year, before output tokens are counted. Those rates are introductory and run until the end of 2026. Sarvam has not disclosed how many GPUs it runs, the utilisation or how much of the traffic is billed at full price. These finer points will decide whether this is a revenue play or a data play. 

Beyond the sovereignty debate, Sarvam offers zero data retention (ZDR) on Token Factory only on request.

ZDR, in simple terms, means not storing any data intentionally after it has served the immediate purpose. Enterprise users of the Sarvam token factory will have to explicitly request ZDR. “Under an agreed ZDR arrangement, prompts and responses are not retained. Operational logs are scoped separately in the terms for your deployment,” the company said in its blog. 

Sarvam will by default use user data to train or fine-tune its models, unless the feature is disabled by the end user. This could be a concern for businesses processing sensitive or proprietary information through the platform.

For Sarvam, the case for Token Factory rests on what global providers cannot easily offer. 

Prompts run on GPUs in India and are not forwarded to overseas servers, which matters to enterprises and government bodies with data-residency requirements. 

Plus, billing is in INR, the platform carries ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II security certifications, and Sarvam promises 99.95% uptime under contract for enterprise deployments. Token Factory also shares credits and API keys with Sarvam’s speech and translation services, and puts its own models in front of developers alongside the ones they already use.

However, the risks are just as visible. The open-weight models Sarvam hosts are available from other Indian providers too. E2E Networks’ Blaze serves DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Gemma, as well as Sarvam’s own models, and Jarvislabs offers a similar catalogue, which leaves price and speed as the main ways to compete. 

The India-hosting advantage is also contested, with OpenAI moving to bring inference to India. And the only usage figure Sarvam has shared is for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which will test whether customers who came for DeepSeek stay for Sarvam’s own models.

India’s Impending Token Factory Boom 

It’s not just Sarvam that has looked to fill the gap. Competition is growing rapidly with anyone who had a hand in the data centre business now jumping on to the inference bandwagon. 

“This is a positive development for the entire ecosystem, indicating to enterprises that operating the models in India is feasible. There is scope for several participants in this market, as the demand for tokens will outgrow any single entity’s capability,” Manoj Dhanda, founder and CEO of Utho Cloud, another player looking to enter the domestic inference space by early 2027. 

Infrastructure giant L&T is building out its AI infrastructure business through Vyoma.AI, with its AI Factory offering spanning data centres, GPU infrastructure, cloud services and model deployment.

Its AI-centric data centres includes a Token Factory designed to provide high-throughput inference, alongside a model garden, AI security and agentic AI services. The company is also offering GPU-as-a-service, managed inference and model customisation.

Similarly, E2E Networks has expanded its AI infrastructure capabilities through the acquisition of identified assets of Jarvislabs, including its intellectual property, hardware, expertise and customer base in August 2025.

Tamil Nadu-based Jarvislabs already offers a Token Factory through which developers can access open-weight models through a common API and pay based on token consumption. Its catalogue includes models from DeepSeek, Gemma, GLM, Nemotron, and Qwen.

“It’s a 2-month-old product, and we have served close to 50B tokens in November and are growing fast. We are seeing customers using it for coding, transcription services, and conversations,” said Vishnu Subramaniam, founder at Jarvislabs. 

To be sure, the company was already serving models through serverless products for more than a year; Subramaniam called the token factory an evolution in that direction. 

Further, more recently, E2E launched Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service that provides access to open models, including Sarvam, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Gemma, through a single OpenAI-compatible API. The service runs on E2E’s Nvidia GPU infrastructure in India, with the company managing model hosting, scaling and optimisation.

Noida-based Utho Cloud plans to deploy 10,000 GPUs between now and 2028. 

“Our infrastructure runs in Tier III and Tier IV data centres inside India, and it is ISO certified,” the company’s CEO said, adding that Utho’s upcoming inference platform will also enable enterprises to comply with norms regarding data residency and transparency on how data is processed, where it travels, and how much it costs per request.

Mirror Security, a cybersecurity firm focused on homomorphic encryption, on the other hand, is approaching the category from a data security standpoint. 

“We provide an encrypted token factory that secures tokens across workflows. We are seeing growing interest among companies in owning their intelligence, giving them greater control over their workloads, token consumption and costs,” said Pankaj Thapa, CEO and cofounder. 

“Our key differentiation is end-to-end encryption. For instance, when you use Claude directly, your prompts are sent in plain text. With our token factory, prompts are sent in an end-to-end encrypted format, while delivering the same responses from the underlying model. There is a marginal latency overhead of around 1–3%, but customers get the benefit of end-to-end encrypted data,” Thapa added.

India As An Inference Hub

For India, the opportunity extends beyond catering to domestic AI adoption. The country’s growing GPU infrastructure, data centre investments and access to a skilled developer ecosystem could help it emerge as a destination for inference workloads serving global customers.

With GPU availability and costs remaining key constraints for AI developers globally, infrastructure providers are looking to improve utilisation by serving multiple models and customers on the same computing infrastructure.

The shift towards token factories could also change the economics of India’s AI infrastructure businesses. Instead of simply renting out GPU capacity, providers can monetise the computing power through managed inference services, while building recurring revenue streams tied to actual usage.

“India can become a place where the world’s tokens are made long before it becomes the place where the leading models are designed, and that is a business worth winning. Three Indian token factories opened between September and November 2026, and six foreign neoclouds have been exploring Indian capacity for inference,” said Gogia.

In the case of Sarvam and other players looking to ride the inference wave, the economics will depend on GPU utilisation, model performance, token pricing, electricity costs and the ability to optimise workloads.

item.title: Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker: Market Cap, Revenue & More
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to…
item.content:encoded:
For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now.

For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation.

Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, PRISM, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses.

The list also includes Indian companies like MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, which are listed on Nasdaq in the US.

India’s startup IPO wave reached its peak in 2025, surpassing the previous year’s momentum.

While 18 startups listed in 2025, 18 startups have already reached that milestone in 2026. With companies like Cult.fit, Razorpay, others, eyeing to tap the public markets this year, the list is only expected to grow further this year.

18 new-age companies — Tonbo Imaging, Zetwerk, AceVector, Moneyview, Rentomojo, ESDS, Purple Style Labs, Turtlemint, Klassroom, Shiprocket, LEAP India, Kissht, Aye Finance, Fractal Analytics, Amagi, Shadowfax, Mobavenue and SEDEMAC — have made their public market debut in 2026.

As of now, the total market capitalisation of the listed companies stands at over $194 Bn.

To consolidate all the information about listed startups, Inc42 has launched the Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker. From the movement in the shares of the companies since their listing to the financial performance of these companies, the tracker is your one-stop resource to know everything you need about the listed tech companies.

Read our methodology here. 

Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride

Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. 

While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges.

While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. Over 60 of the new-age tech companies are currently profitable.

In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. 

It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s purview are about a decade old. 

From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra’s IPO materialised within four years of its operations.  

Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal.

Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr

Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom

The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem.

The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups.

While fintech and ecommerce house 14 names each, 13 enterprise tech startups have listed on the bourses so far. 

The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of Tonbo Imaging, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts.

Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups

While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 27 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru’s ninetineen and Mumbai’s fifteen. 

While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. 

Delhi NCR contributes $104 Bn in the cumulative $193 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies. 

Last updated: Nov 21
The Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker will be updated periodically with fresh data.

item.title: Fi Money Manages To Cut FY26 Loss By 25%To ₹153.3 Cr, Revenue Sinks 21%
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Following an extended period of turbulence, fintech startup Fi Money managed to narrow its consolidated net loss for the fiscal…
item.content:encoded:
Following an extended period of turbulence, fintech startup Fi Money managed to narrow its consolidated net loss for the fiscal year FY26 by 25% to ₹153.3 Cr from ₹204.4 Cr loss incurred in the previous year. 

However, the reduction in its loss appears to be a signal of shrinking scale rather than improving profitability. The startup’s operating revenue shrunk by 21.1% YoY to ₹38.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹49 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹15.7 Cr, its total income for the period totalled ₹54.3 Cr. 

After accounting for total tax expense of ₹7.3 Lakh and other comprehensive income of ₹59.9 Lakh, the company’s total comprehensive loss stood at ₹152.7 Cr in FY26. 

Founded in 2019 by ex-Google Pay executives Sumit Gwalani and Sujith Narayanan, Fi Money started off as a neobank offering savings accounts, loans, investments and wealth products. It allowed users to track spending, set up automatic savings schemes, make UPI payments, and pay bills as well. 

While lending turned out to be a cash cow, by 2025, it was struggling to monetise most of its other verticals and kept burning capital on user acquisition. Facing an existential crisis, it had to resort to heavy personnel cuts to control costs. 

Subsequently, the troubled startup said it would pivot from a consumer-facing neobank and focus on B2B AI and enterprise tech offerings. It ended its banking partnership with Federal Bank and discontinued those services. Cofounder Gwalani also exited to build his own enterprise AI startup. 

Where Did Fi Money Spend?

In line with shrinking top line, the fintech startup’s total expenses for the fiscal fell 22.8% to ₹207.5 Cr from ₹268.9 Cr a year ago. Let’s take a closer look at its expenses: 

  • Employee Benefit Expense: Personnel related expenditure fell 38.8% YoY to ₹77.1 Cr in FY26.
  • IT Expenses: Fi spent ₹27.4 Cr on IT infrastructure and platform costs in FY26, a 30.1% reduction from ₹39.2 Cr in the previous year. 
  • Contract Charges: The startup paid ₹18.4 Cr to third-party contract services in the year under review, 25.8% lower compared to ₹24.8 Cr in FY25. 
  • Advertising And Sales Promotion: Marketing, customer acquisition, and promotions cost it ₹14 Cr in FY26, a sharp reduction from ₹36.5 Cr spent in FY25.

item.title: Traya’s FY26 Revenue Jumps 73% YoY To ₹585 Cr, Loss Up 23%
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Haircare brand Traya’s top line zoomed significantly in the fiscal year FY26, crossing the ₹500 Cr threshold. The Fireside-backed startup’s…
item.content:encoded:
Haircare brand Traya’s top line zoomed significantly in the fiscal year FY26, crossing the ₹500 Cr threshold. The Fireside-backed startup’s operating revenue jumped about 73% to ₹585.1 Cr from ₹338.4 Cr in the previous fiscal.

Including other income of ₹8.2 Cr, Traya’s total income stood at ₹593.2 Cr in FY26, up 72.9% annually. Other income more than doubled from ₹4.6 Cr in the previous fiscal.

However, the startup’s net loss for the fiscal also increased 23.4% to ₹29 Cr from ₹23.5 Cr in FY25.

Traya reported an EBITDA loss of approximately ₹28.1 Cr in FY26, compared with an estimated EBITDA loss of ₹21.2 Cr in FY25. EBITDA margin stood at -4.81% in FY26, against -6.25% in the previous fiscal.

Founded in 2019 by Saloni Anand and Altaf Saiyed, Traya offers customised haircare solutions, using technology to identify customers’ specific hair loss triggers. The startup says it combines hair assessment, recommendation algorithm, and doctor approval to develop personalised treatment plans.

Traya competes with brands like Arata, Vedix, SkinKraft, and Ravel Care, in the broader haircare and personalised beauty market.

It sells its products via its app, website and other major ecommerce platforms like Amazon and Flipkart. Alongside its online business, Traya has been expanding its offline presence and currently operates more than 20 centres across Pune, Mumbai, Nagpur, and Hyderabad.

The startup, which counts investors like Xponentia Capital, Kae Capital as its backers, is in talks to raise around ₹300 Cr (about $31 Mn) from Belgium-based investment firm Verlinvest, Inc42 reported exclusively in October. The proposed round would value the startup at ₹2,500 Cr (about $262 Mn) to ₹3,000 Cr (about $315 Mn).

Zooming Into Traya’s FY26 Spending

The startup’s expenses grew 70.5% to ₹623.2 Cr during the year from ₹365.5 Cr in FY25, outpacing its total income and contributing to the higher losses. Here is a closer look at where Traya spent the most:

  • Sales And Marketing Expenses: The startup spent 44.1% of its overall expenses towards sales and marketing, which stood at ₹275.1 Cr, up 99.9% from the previous year’s cost of ₹137.6 Cr.
  • Purchase of Stock-In-Trade: Spending under this head rose 80.7% to ₹146 Cr in the year under review, compared to ₹80.8 Cr in FY25.
  • Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs rose 42.6% to ₹81 Cr in FY26, from ₹56.8 Cr in the previous year.
