item.title: Google Commits $5 Mn To Sundar Pichai’s Alma Mater IIT Kharagpur
item.dc:creator: Zakariya Khan
item.description: Google announced a commitment of  $5 Mn in funding to IIT Kharagpur, the alma mater of CEO Sundar Pichai, to…
item.content:encoded:
Google announced a commitment of  $5 Mn in funding to IIT Kharagpur, the alma mater of CEO Sundar Pichai, to accelerate advanced artificial intelligence (AI) research, expand AI education and strengthen the institute’s technological capabilities.

Announcing this, Pichai said the collaboration would help shape the next generation of students, adding that India was increasingly emerging as a hub for innovation.

“Looking forward to seeing this collaboration shape the path for the next generation of students, just as IIT Kharagpur shaped my own. India is increasingly at the forefront of innovation; programmes like this will help implement PM Modi’s vision that the benefits of AI reach everyone in India,” he said in a LinkedIn post.

The funding is intended to support research into the application of AI across Indic languages, materials science, agriculture and educational technology. It will also help expand AI training and curriculum development for students, faculty members and teachers. However, no concrete plans on how exactly the cash would be used is yet to be decided. 

Besides, Google has also said that it will support development of AI frameworks and tools to strengthen the institute’s technological ecosystem and research capabilities.

The latest commitment builds on Google’s existing research collaboration with IIT Kharagpur under its Amplify Initiative which was announced last year. That initiative focuses on developing hyperlocal datasets that could capture India’s linguistic diversity. The datasets are intended to improve the representation of Indian languages and regional contexts in large language models (LLMs).

The collaboration also covers datasets for specific use cases, including healthcare and safety, across multiple Indic languages. It aims to address gaps in existing AI models, which often lack sufficient regional language data and cultural context.

Google’s AI Investments In India’s Academic Ecosystem

Google has made several funding commitments to Indian academic and research institutions as it looks to expand AI research, talent development and real-world applications of the technology.

In November 2025, the company committed $8 Mn to four AI Centres of Excellence established by the Indian government at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bengaluru, IIT Kanpur, IIT Madras and IIT Ropar.

The funding was aimed at supporting AI research across healthcare, urban governance, education and agriculture. Google separately announced a $2 Mn contribution to establish an Indic Language Technologies Research Hub at IIT Bombay.

In January 2026, the tech giant announced an ₹85 Cr grant to Wadhwani AI to scale AI-powered learning initiatives. The programme aims to reach 75 Mn students, 1.8 Mn educators and 1 Mn early-career professionals by December 2027.

Beyond academic partnerships, Google has also been backing AI-led climate and sustainability initiatives in India.

The company recently selected four Indian startups — Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests and Climitra Carbon — for its inaugural Google DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet (APAC). The three-month programme provides startups with access to Google’s AI models, technical support and expert mentorship to develop solutions for environmental challenges.

item.title: Scaler Cofounder Anshuman Singh Unveils AI Training Data Venture Arcfront
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Tech upskilling platform Scaler’s cofounder Anshuman Singh has unveiled Arcfront, an AI research and training data venture that turns records…
item.content:encoded:
Tech upskilling platform Scaler’s cofounder Anshuman Singh has unveiled Arcfront, an AI research and training data venture that turns records of how professionals solve problems into material for training and testing advanced AI models.

Singh is building the venture with Naman Bhalla, Scaler’s former head of AI products and an ex-Google software engineer. In a post on X, Singh said Arcfront also has “deep support” from Scaler cofounder Abhimanyu Saxena.

Singh claimed that four of the five frontier AI labs became Arcfront’s customers within less than a year of operations. However, he did not identify the labs. 

Arcfront operates under Evaratus Inc., according to its website’s legal disclosures. Company recruitment material identifies Evaratus as formerly Scaler AI Labs, Scaler’s frontier AI research and engineering division. 

Scaler’s privacy policy also lists Scaler AI Labs Inc. among its group companies. However, the public disclosures reviewed do not establish Evaratus’ current shareholding or whether the business has been separated from the Scaler group.

Inc42 has reached out to Arcfront’s founders for clarity on its ownership structure and relationship with Scaler. The story will be updated based on their response.

Singh’s LinkedIn profile lists November 2025 as the end of his tenure at Scaler and the start of his work on Arcfront. Bhalla’s profile indicates that he began working on the venture around the same time. However, it remains unclear whether Singh retains any operational responsibilities at Scaler or how the transition relates to Scaler AI Labs’ subsequent identity as Evaratus. 

Turning Expertise Into Data

Arcfront’s proposition centres on the gap between AI models’ ability to solve structured problems and their performance in workplace situations requiring context, judgement, and decisions involving competing trade-offs.

Singh argued that models capable of solving difficult coding and mathematical problems can still struggle when placed in professional roles such as finance management.

Arcfront aims to address this by working with organisations to reconstruct how experts reach decisions, including the options they reject, revisions they make, and eventual outcomes. 

The startup calls this approach ‘Decision Arc Data’. It converts these records into training data, reinforcement learning environments, and evaluations for frontier AI labs. 

Reinforcement learning environments allow models to practise tasks and receive feedback on their results. Its work covers software engineering, site reliability engineering, cybersecurity, and collaborative workplace tasks. It also builds sector-specific evaluations using workflows from healthcare, life sciences, legal services, and finance to identify where models fail.

Separately, angel investor and former Google, Facebook, and DoorDash executive Gokul Rajaram identified Arcfront as the company behind his earlier claim about a startup reaching a $1 Bn annualised revenue run rate faster than any other company.

In the earlier post, Rajaram said the unnamed company had no revenue in November 2025 and generated $80 Mn in September 2026, putting it on course to reach a $1 Bn annualised run rate within 11 months of starting operations.

The AI Data Opportunity

Arcfront joins a growing group of startups building training datasets, testing tools, and simulated work environments for AI developers.

For instance, Deccan AI raised $25 Mn in March to expand its post-training data offerings, research, and enterprise infrastructure. Its products include reinforcement learning environments that recreate enterprise workflows and failure scenarios, allowing AI agents to practise before deployment in business operations.

A related opportunity is emerging in physical AI, where startups collect recordings of human activity to train robots. Startups including Human Archive are building data pipelines using footage of workers performing physical tasks. 

Earlier this week, Humyn Labs raised $47 Mn, comprising $26 Mn in equity and $21 Mn in venture debt, to expand its data collection and robot deployment operations.

The opportunity has also drawn founders from India’s consumer internet ecosystem. Pronto founder Anjali Sardana recently launched San Francisco-based Provision Labs to collect data for training and testing physical AI systems.

item.content:encoded:
Adding to the growing threats of cyber attacks, SaaS startup MoEngage has now suffered a cybersecurity breach.

The attack involved unauthorised access to a limited part of the startup’s cloud infrastructure via a compromised third-party vendor account. 

Some customers reportedly faced difficulties accessing the platform for nearly seven days, according to a report by ET. However, MoEngage denied any disruption in its services. It claimed to have identified and contained the incident in late October. It said that it engaged independent cybersecurity experts to validate its findings, remediated the breach and strengthened its security measures.

“Fewer than 1% of our customer accounts were affected, and we have notified each of them directly. There was no disruption to our services as a result of this incident,” MoEngage said.

The incident comes amid growing concerns around cybersecurity risks arising from third-party service providers and vulnerabilities across interconnected digital infrastructure.

Recent disruptions involving technology companies and large enterprises, including Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), have renewed attention on the resilience of global digital infrastructure amid the growing threat of AI.

In this light, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora warned that AI makes it easier for hackers to target multiple organisations simultaneously. AI can accelerate reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities and enable attackers to scale their operations across several targets.

A key point of entry for compromising major software infrastructures has been their interaction with third-party vendors. Smaller service providers do not maintain security standards comparable to those of their enterprise clients. Compromising a single tech provider can potentially expose multiple organisations that rely on its services.

Founded in 2014 by Raviteja Dodda and Yashwanth Kumar, MoEngage provides customer engagement, analytics and messaging software that enables businesses to communicate with users through mobile notifications, email, SMS, WhatsApp and in-app messages.

Headquartered in Bengaluru and San Francisco, the company claims to serve over 1,350 enterprises across 75 countries.

MoEngage is also preparing for a potential public listing in India. 

In January 2026, the National Company Law Tribunal approved the reverse merger of its US-based parent, MoEngage Inc, into its Indian arm, MoEngage India Private Limited, as part of its corporate restructuring ahead of a potential domestic listing.

item.title: Exclusive: Celcius Logistics Eyes ₹100 Cr To Expand Cold Chain Network
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Cold-chain logistics provider Celcius Logistics is in advanced talks to raise ₹100 Cr in a Pre-Series C funding round from…
item.content:encoded:
Cold-chain logistics provider Celcius Logistics is in advanced talks to raise ₹100 Cr in a Pre-Series C funding round from existing investors IvyCap Ventures, Omnivore, and Eurazeo, alongside new investor wealthtech platform Centricity, sources told Inc42.

The proposed round is expected to comprise equity and debt, the sources said.

The startup plans to use the capital to strengthen its technology infrastructure, expand its presence across India, and scale its pharma and hyperlocal logistics businesses, the sources added. 

Celcius is also looking to raise a Series C funding round by mid-2027. 

Inc42 has reached out to Celcius for comments on the development. The story will be updated on receiving a response.

The funding talks follow Celcius’ ₹250 Cr Series B round in May 2025, which comprised equity and debt. Eurazeo and Omnivore co-led the equity component, with participation from IvyCap Ventures. 

At the time, Celcius said it would use the debt to meet working capital requirements, while the equity would support expansion into Tier III and IV markets and industries such as pharmaceuticals. 

Founded in 2020 by Swarup Bose, Rajneesh Raman, and Arbind Jain, Celcius operates a digital platform that connects shippers with transporters and cold storage providers. It centralises bookings and shipment data for temperature-controlled transportation and storage.

The startup serves businesses across quick commerce, ecommerce, agriculture, and healthcare, transporting temperature-sensitive products such as pharmaceuticals and fresh produce. 

Its specialised verticals include pharma-focused Celcius+ and Celcius Green, which provides refrigerated last-mile deliveries using electric vehicles. 

Celcius has over 50 distribution hubs and a presence in more than 200 additional cities over the preceding year.

The startup competes with cold-chain logistics players including Indicold and JustDeliveries, both of which raised funding in 2024.
Celcius’ expansion comes amid gaps in India’s cold-chain infrastructure. According to a FICCI–Grant Thornton Bharat report, India had 40.22 Mn tonnes of cold storage capacity across 8,815 facilities by June 2025, with about three-quarters of the capacity used for potatoes.

According to the report, India loses between 17 Mn and 47 Mn tonnes of horticultural, dairy, meat, poultry, and fish products annually across the value chain. It identified gaps in packhouses, pre-cooling facilities, refrigerated transport, and ripening chambers.

A decade ago, India’s startup landscape barely registered on the global radar. Today, it stands as the world’s third-largest startup ecosystem, home to 2.62 Lakh startups, 133 unicorns and 156 soonicorns that have redefined scale in emerging markets.

As unicorns mature and soonicorns inch closer to the billion-dollar mark, a new breed of startups is quietly rising — the minicorns. Valued between $100 Mn and $200 Mn, they form the crucial bridge between early growth and market leadership, offering a window into India’s next wave of scalable, capital-efficient innovation.

After the Unicorn and Soonicorn Trackers, we present the Minicorn Tracker — mapping the next generation of disruptors shaping India’s startup landscape.

According to Inc42’s analysis, the country is now home to 71 minicorns, startups valued between $100 Mn and $200 Mn, with a combined market capitalisation of more than $9.3 Bn. These companies have raised over $3.2 Bn in funding since inception.

Fintech Home To The Highest Minicorns

Much like the unicorn and soonicorn landscape, fintech and ecommerce also command the most dominant presence in the minicorn ecosystem space too. Fintech overtook ecommerce over the past few months with 13 minicorns against 12 ecommerce minicorns. Olyv was the most recent startup to attain the minicorn tag. 

Trailing behind fintech, ecommerce, houses minicorns like Bombay Shaving Company, DailyObjects, Foxtale, among others.

While fintech and ecommerce continue to dominate the minicorn realm, India’s AI industry is fast catching up. The sector takes the third spot in the minicorn club, housing eight startups. The most valued minicorn, Different ($194 Mn) is also an AI startup.

The advanced technology & hardware sector, which is constituted with segments like deeptech, defence tech, and spacetech, houses 7 startups. Enterprise tech also houses a similar number of sub-$200 Mn ventures.

Bengaluru Remains The Top Hub For Future Unicorns

Bengaluru leads the city-wise distribution with 24 minicorns, followed by Delhi NCR with 20. Together, the two hubs account for 44 of the 71 companies in the tracker.

Mumbai ranks third with 12 minicorns, while Pune and Chennai account for five and four companies, respectively.

Bengaluru’s minicorns include AppsForBharat, CoreEL Technologies, Kapiva, Kiwi, QpiAI, Swish and Zolostays. Delhi NCR is home to companies such as Arisinfra Solutions, Bombay Shaving Company, CollegeDekho, Farmley, Masters’ Union and Unicommerce.

Mumbai-based minicorns include FINO Payment Bank, Foxtale, LiquiLoans, Snapmint, The Souled Store, Traya and Wonderchef.

Electric two-wheeler maker River Mobility’s operating revenue jumped 4.2X to ₹432.3 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 from ₹101.9 Cr in FY25.

However, the Bengaluru-based startup’s net loss widened 46% to ₹285.7 Cr from ₹195.7 Cr amid a ramp-up in scooter production and sales. Total expenses increased 140.1% to ₹719.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹299.5 Cr in the previous year.

Including other income, River’s total income stood at ₹433.4 Cr compared with ₹103.8 Cr in FY25. Its net cash outflow from operating activities increased to ₹235.5 Cr from ₹160.1 Cr.

Sales of escooters contributed ₹353.4 Cr to operating revenue, including government subsidies, compared with ₹81.3 Cr in FY25. Revenue from services, primarily the design and development of prototypes, rose to ₹57.7 Cr from ₹18.1 Cr.

Scaling Sales & Distribution

River was India’s seventh-largest E2W maker by registrations in October, with a market share of about 3%, according to Vahan data.

Its registrations rose 15.7% MoM to 6,533 units in October from 5,647 units in September, according to Vahan data. For context, it sold 24,492 EVs in the entire FY26, which was up 5X from 4,906 units sold in the previous fiscal.

Founded in 2021 by Aravind Mani and Vipin George, River launched its Indie escooter in February 2023 and began sales in October that year. The startup has positioned the scooter around utility, including for entrepreneurs who need to carry tools and equipment.

Mani told Inc42 in April last year that River would need to sell 15,000-20,000 units a month to achieve EBITDA breakeven.

Following the close of FY26, River announced a $120 Mn Series C round in August, co-led by Elev8 Venture Partners and Claypond Capital. The round marked its first fundraise from Indian investors. Before that, it had raised $68 Mn in equity funding, including a $40 Mn round led by Yamaha Motor.

River plans to expand capacity at its existing factory near Bengaluru and build a greenfield facility. It also plans to introduce products in the utility lifestyle segment. At the time of the August fundraise, it had more than 75 stores and was targeting over 350 by March 2028.

Inside River’s Expense Bill

Raw Material Costs: Its largest expense head rose over 251% to ₹404.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹115 Cr in FY25 as it ramped up operations.

Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs increased 47% to ₹110.9 Cr from ₹75.5 Cr.

Testing Expense: Similarly, its cost of testing vehicles shot up 150% YoY in FY26 to ₹48.5 Cr from ₹19.4 Cr in the year-ago period due to the rise in sales and building a new product pipeline. 

Advertising & Business Promotion: The startup spent ₹28.3 Cr on advertising in FY26, a 117.7% increase from ₹13 Cr in the previous year.

item.title: Fintechs Bear The Brunt As Yes Bank Upgrades AI Safeguards
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Fintech platforms have emerged as an unlikely collateral damage as Yes Bank strengthens its defences against AI-driven cyberattacks. Sources told…
item.content:encoded:
Fintech platforms have emerged as an unlikely collateral damage as Yes Bank strengthens its defences against AI-driven cyberattacks.

Sources told Inc42 that the cybersecurity upgrades at Yes Bank are disrupting workflows and delaying payouts at payment service providers. 

One fintech executive said that his platform was facing issues ever since Yes Bank sent an email, which noted that the bank was “implementing enhanced precautionary measures to safeguard” transactions. The fintech was subsequently also informed that the bank was making changes to its banking APIs, which was delaying settlements.

These changes, in turn, are impacting payment processing and settlement timelines for some businesses that rely on banking APIs to move funds.

Another industry insider noted that the issues began to crop up after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued directives to banks and other financial institutions to bolster their cybersecurity defences. According to the source quoted above, the RBI directions came after the recent cyberattack on the State Bank of India (SBI), referring to the data leak at the bank in October.

The RBI is also said to have directed the banks and other financial institutions to ensure the funds of customers are not impacted by the growing wave of AI-assisted cyberattacks.

Inc42 has reached out to Yes Bank for a comment on the matter. This story will be updated upon receiving their response.

This comes as multiple Indian crypto exchanges continue to grapple with delays in processing withdrawals due to disruptions at its banking partners. Coinbase India paused all withdrawals last week, before partially resuming payouts, citing an outage at its banking partner.

CoinDCX, which has also been facing similar issues, claimed that upgrades at “most” of its partner banks was delaying the processing of INR withdrawals. Zebpay also said that payouts were taking longer than usual because of a technical disruption at its banking partner.

Earlier yesterday, Razorpay told its customers that it to delay merchant settlements temporarily due to a technical issue at a partner bank. However, the IPO-bound unicorn reinstated the service hours later.

The development came on the day CERT-In issued an alarm over unauthorised transactions at technology service providers for banks and other financial institutions. 

Bank Vendors Under AI Attack

In an advisory, the cybersecurity watchdog flagged that malicious actors were using AI-driven cyberattacks to undertake unauthorised transactions at technology service providers, which handle government-linked payment processes, as well as platforms handling vendor payouts.

CERT-In said that attackers altered business records or approval relationships and ​then used legitimate payment processes to approve fraudulent transactions. The watchdog did not elaborate on how much money of the proceeds had been funneled out. 

The cybersecurity agency said that the reported incidents involved cyberattackers misusing business applications and workflows, rather than direct exploitation of payment APIs alone. As per CERT-In, these attackers used trusted systems to process unauthorised transactions and  exploited gaps in verification and reconciliation of changes to business records.

CERT-In also noted that it has identified the following techniques used by attackers for perpetrating AI-assisted cyberattacks against fintech platforms:

  • Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services and possible attack paths
  • Rapid preparation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including through analysis of software updates and related technical information
  • Use of multiple agents or automated workers to undertake reconnaissance, privilege discovery and other intrusion tasks in parallel
  • Modification of scripts, requests and attack steps in response to errors, blocked attempts or information returned by targeted systems
  • Use of valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships and external infrastructure to gain further access.

As such, CERT-In also directed government entities to identify and restrict accounts and integrations that can approve payments or change payment-related records. 

Besides recommending undertaking independent certification for high-risk changes to payment records, it also called on the banks to reconcile critical business data maintained by service providers against authoritative records. 

It also called on the TSPS to restrict administrative accounts and control-plane privileges. CERT-In also directed fintechs to review unusual activity and monitor changes to payment-related business records.
